newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to meet PM, trains guns on tax-dodgers.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to meet PM, trains guns on tax-dodgers.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will hold talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday, his second working day in the Kremlin after nearly two months spent convalescing from open heart surgery.
Yeltsin, keen to show he is firmly back in control, has pledged resolute leadership in tackling the many problems that have accumulated during his prolonged absence.

"I am in a good mood, I feel well and am generally ready for battle," a smiling president, shielded from subzero temperatures by a fur hat and long overcoat, told reporters on Monday as he returned to his office.

Chernomyrdin, who assumed many of Yeltsin's responsibilities during his illness, will brief the president on the political and economic situation in the country. The two men are expected to meet around midday (0900 GMT).
The 65-year-old Yeltsin, dogged by ill health, has spent very little time in the Kremlin since being re-elected for a second term in July. He had a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5.
One of Yeltsin's main tasks this week will be chairing Thursday's session of a special commission set up to improve tax collection and boost flagging state revenues.
The session will be devoted to Russia's pensioners, who are owed up to 14 trillion roubles ($2.5 billion) in unpaid pensions, Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin told reporters.

Millions of state and private-sector workers have also not been paid for months and many are on the breadline. The government blames tax dodgers for the delays and has vowed to crack down on both corporate and individual offenders.
Yeltsin recently said managers of firms that did not pay their taxes were unfit for the job and should be sacked.
"The only criterion here is the people's quality of life. We will part with those who are unable to turn towards the people. We need new impulses, we need more courage and energy," he said.
But despite speculation in the Russian media, Yeltsin apparently does not plan any immediate changes in his entourage.
RIA news agency quoted his spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying the president was satisfied with the work of his staff during his absence.

Yeltsin held talks on Monday with senior aides, including Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais -- a hate figure for the communists and nationalists who dominate Russia's State Duma lower house of parliament.

Opposition deputies had initially called for Chubais's sacking as a condition for supporting the government's 1997 budget plans but they are now expected to approve the draft in the near future on its third and final Duma reading.
Despite the Duma's new-found willingness to cooperate with the government over its draft budget, Russia remains in the economic doldrums five years after ditching communism.
Official data released on Monday showed gross domestic product (GDP) shrank another six percent in 1996, confounding more optimistic forecasts made at the start of the year.
Yuri Yurkov, chairman of the State Statistics Committee, dampened hopes of any swift improvement.

"Nineteen ninety-seven is not sure to bring an investment boom," he told a news conference on Monday, adding that both foreign and Russian investors were still deterred by political and economic uncertainty.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said the president's return to the helm would make little difference anyway.
"Yeltsin is in no condition to resolve even a single issue facing Russia today," he said.
